disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c is in the diabetes range, and with an obese BMI, current smoking, regular alcohol use, and existing heart and blood pressure conditions, your overall risk picture is significant. The most valuable next steps are completing the highlighted tests—lipid profile, kidney function, eye exam, foot exam, blood pressure, and cardiovascular risk assessment—along with building in regular, doctor-approved physical activity and following the DASH-style, low-sodium eating pattern described in your diet plan. Making steady progress on these areas, together with your care team, can meaningfully support your long-term health.

risk_factors.label: Existing health condition: Heart or blood-vessel disease
Existing health condition: High blood pressure

comorbidity_assessment.note: Higher blood sugar can add extra strain on blood vessels already affected by heart disease, so keeping sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol in a healthy range together is especially important for you.

Blood sugar and blood pressure often influence each other, and both raise strain on the heart and kidneys, so monitoring and managing them together can be more protective than addressing either alone.

foods_to_eat: Vegetables like spinach, bottle gourd, and carrots
Whole grains such as brown rice, oats, and millets
Pulses like moong, rajma, and chana
Fish such as rohu and pomfret
Low-fat dairy or curd in small amounts
Nuts and seeds like almonds and walnuts
Fresh fruits such as guava, papaya, and apple
foods_to_avoid: Deep-fried foods like pakoras and samosas
Refined flour products like white bread and maida-based snacks
Excess added salt and salty condiments
plan.portion_guidance: Aim for balanced meals with half a plate of vegetables, a quarter plate of whole grains, and a quarter plate of protein such as fish, dal, or tofu. Use katoris and bowls to measure portions and avoid second servings of rice or roti.
plan.hydration: Drink about 8 to 10 glasses of water daily. Limit alcohol intake, and avoid sugary or salty packaged drinks. Herbal teas or plain buttermilk can be refreshing alternatives.

exercise: Before starting any new or vigorous activity, get medical clearance from your doctor given your heart condition and blood pressure.
Begin with gentle, low-intensity activities such as short walks, and build up gradually over several weeks.
Aim to work towards at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, spread across most days, once cleared by your doctor.
Add simple muscle-strengthening activities (like light resistance bands or bodyweight exercises) on 2 days a week once you are ready.
Stop exercising right away and seek medical help if you feel chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with 10 minutes of gentle walking, 5 days a week, and slowly build up to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, as your fitness and comfort allow.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the obese range, so gradually working towards a healthier weight can help your heart health and blood sugar levels. Focus on steady, sustainable changes rather than quick fixes, and build habits you can maintain long-term.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, avoid screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet to support restful sleep.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5 to 10 minutes a day to help calm your body and mind.
Try mindfulness or relaxation exercises, such as guided meditation apps, a few times a week.
Make time for activities you enjoy, like spending time with family or hobbies, to help manage daily stress.
behaviour_change: Since you currently smoke, consider stopping smoking for the sake of your heart and blood pressure. Support options include calling a quitline, speaking with your doctor about support programmes, and using nicotine replacement products if advised by a health professional.
Since you drink regularly, consider cutting down on alcohol, as this can help manage your blood pressure and overall health. Try setting clear limits and having alcohol-free days each week.
Keep track of your progress with small, achievable goals for activity, sleep and stress, and celebrate steady improvements rather than aiming for perfection.
Build a support network, whether through family, friends or a health professional, to help you stay motivated with these changes.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

preventive_actions: Schedule the highlighted tests soon, especially lipid profile, kidney function, eye exam, and cardiovascular risk assessment.
Work with a tobacco cessation resource or your doctor to create a plan to reduce or stop smoking.
Limit alcohol intake, since it can affect blood sugar control and interact with heart and blood pressure health.
Keep daily sodium under 2,300 mg and reduce salty, processed foods like pickles and papad.
Aim for regular moderate aerobic activity once you have medical clearance, building up gradually.
Track your home blood pressure readings and bring them to your next doctor visit.
